renders.prompt: Explain the argument of this song as if to a bright 10-year-old. Short words. Concrete images. No jargon, no Sanskrit terms, no meta-commentary.

paragraphs.text: Make a list of the body: skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, bones — and it stays sick anyway, always fooled. Māyā, you dunk the ones who know and the ones who don't, and they never learn how great you are.
Gods bolted into metal pictures — people look and go hā hā, what a waste. If you're proud of owning a body that owns an I, what foolery won't Mother Māyā cook up for you?
Everything born of fun-and-games delusion — emptied brains, I-covered bodies, the whole lot. Keep me from falling, highest goddess — you who are made of knowing yourself, born of trying.
Look at her: scary, scarier, not scary at all. Called higher and lower, neither one nor the other. Śiva's power in every shape you can think of — just watch it, and sit down inside your own wow.
You live right between high and low, in the middle of their rays — and I don't cling to a single call about what is, what isn't, what is-and-isn't.
Your top shape flashes, Mother — and so does the other one, the world-shaped one. Remember them both, good people: she scares you safe and she gives you gifts. Top goddess, both ways.
Lady of the five-act play, made of top knowing, Pārvatī — please be kind. Pick up the kid who fell into the beast-trap. Hush the little one with cool glances.
First bow: the masters who got there first, the gods, the goddess, then the yogins. Then the credits: these fifteen verses were spoken by Abhinavagupta.
